chunks: And as for what was narrated: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from al-Barqi from Sa'd ibn Sa'd al-Ash'ari from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about eating the meat of chickens in the stables, while they are not prevented from anything that passes by the excrement, mixed with it, and eating their eggs, so he said, 'There is no harm in it.'

This report does not contradict what we have previously mentioned from the reports, because the report does not state that they are 'Jallalah' (animals fed on excrement), but rather that they pass by the excrement and are not prevented from anything, and all of that does not indicate that they are Jallalah.

And if the report explicitly stated that they are Jallalah, it would be permissible for us to interpret it, saying that his saying (peace be upon him) 'There is no harm in it' implies that they should be purified (istibra') after three days, according to what we have previously mentioned.
And we did not say that the meat of Jallalah animals is forbidden in all cases.
Rather, we said that the purification to be observed is the one we mentioned if its food is not mixed with other than excrement; but if it is mixed, then there is no harm in eating its meat.
Thus, on this basis, there is no contradiction between the reports, and this has been narrated.

key_terms.الِاسْتِبْرَاء: Purification period (waiting for the impure food to leave the body)
key_terms.جَلَّالَة: An animal fed primarily on excrement or impure waste
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ بِهِ: There is no harm in it (permissible)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on eating chicken fed on excrement (Jallalah) in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from Imam al-Rida (AS), the permissibility of consuming Jallalah (animals fed on excrement) is clarified by distinguishing between the animal's state and the purity of its feed; the Imam suggests that 'no harm' may imply a brief purification period or apply specifically when the feed is mixed with excrement rather than being purely excremental. This nuanced interpretation resolves apparent contradictions in hadith literature by aligning the ruling with the principle that impurity in the food source, rather than the animal itself, dictates the prohibition. The discussion highlights the Shia scholarly method of reconciling texts through contextual interpretation (ta'wil) and specific conditions.
